one_liner: Meta's RocksDB (LSM-tree) storage engine for MySQL: ~4x smaller on disk, ~5x InnoDB's TPC-C tps when cache is tiny.
what_it_does: MyRocks is a MySQL storage engine (ENGINE=RocksDB) that stores tables and indexes in RocksDB instead of InnoDB's B+tree pages. It lives in storage/rocksdb/ of Meta's MySQL fork (branches fb-mysql-5.6.35 through fb-mysql-8.0.32), with RocksDB pulled in as a git submodule. The SQL layer, client protocol and binlog replication are unchanged. You create or ALTER tables to ENGINE=RocksDB and can place each index in its own column family through the index COMMENT ('cf_name', or 'rev:cf_name' for a reverse-ordered family). It is a whole database server, not a library you link.
how_it_is_fast: Every index is a key range in RocksDB, prefixed by a 4-byte index id. Keys are encoded in a memcmp-comparable ('mem-comparable') form, so the bytewise comparator orders them. The primary key maps to the full row (a clustered layout), and each secondary key embeds the PK. Writes go to a WAL and an in-memory MemTable and are later flushed and compacted into sorted, block-compressed SST files (leveled compaction; LZ4 on upper levels, ZSTD recommended at the bottom). That means no in-place page rewrites, no doublewrite buffer and no padding of compressed pages to 8KB. Non-unique secondary indexes are maintained with blind Put/SingleDelete and no read-before-write, and prefix bloom filters plus the block cache limit read amplification. In Percona's run this showed up as I/O. At a 5GB cache InnoDB wrote ~245k KB/s and spent 57% of its time in iowait, while MyRocks wrote ~87k KB/s and was CPU-bound (56% us + 11% sy). Derived from the page's tables, that is ~21 KB written per transaction for MyRocks at every cache size, vs ~288 KB for InnoDB at 5GB.
when_to_use: OLTP on SSD where the dataset is several times larger than RAM. With a 90GB (InnoDB-sized) TPC-C dataset, MyRocks delivered 4.95x InnoDB's tps at 5GB of cache, 2.4x at 20GB and 1.16x at 50GB (ratios derived from the page's table).

Storage cost or flash wear is the constraint. Meta's user database (UDB) migration cut instance size by 62.3% vs compressed InnoDB and bytes written by 75% (one replica set: 2187.4GB vs 824.4GB, 13.34 vs 3.42 MB/s written), at slightly lower CPU.

Insert- or update-heavy tables with several non-unique secondary indexes, or loading new tables. rocksdb_bulk_load ingests SST files straight into the bottom level; Meta measured 2.2x (1 table) to 5.7x (20 parallel tables) InnoDB's load rate.
Cloud instances where memory and IOPS are billed. Throughput barely changes from a 5GB to a 100GB cache (4206 to 4599 tps), so you can run small-memory instances.
Your application already runs under READ-COMMITTED with row-based binlog, no foreign keys, and mostly PK or prefix lookups with forward range scans (Meta's social-graph pattern).
when_not_to_use: The working set fits in the buffer pool. InnoDB overtakes at 60GB (4757 vs 4571 tps) and is ~1.30x faster at 80-100GB (5985 vs 4617, 5961 vs 4599). MyRocks still reads ~13.7 KB per transaction at 100GB vs ~0.3 KB for InnoDB (derived), which is LSM read amplification.

You need InnoDB features it lacks: FOREIGN KEY, fulltext and spatial indexes, SAVEPOINT, EXCHANGE PARTITION, transportable tablespaces, gap/next-key locks, statement or mixed binlog format, Group Replication, the Clone plugin, multi-valued indexes or table encryption (per the Meta wiki and Percona's current docs). Only READ-COMMITTED and REPEATABLE-READ are accepted (the source rejects the other levels).

Big single transactions. All uncommitted changes stay in memory, and a transaction is capped by rocksdb_max_row_locks (default 1,048,576). Open issue #194 measures many-row statements at 7-10x InnoDB's time (for example, updating an indexed column on 1M rows took 99.5 s vs 12.4 s), and Percona warns that a large ALTER ... ENGINE=RocksDB can be OOM-killed unless you use bulk-load mode.

You are sensitive to latency jitter. Percona saw periodic 1-second throughput drops it could not explain, the data directory swung from 20GB to 31GB between compactions, and the tuning wiki says compaction without a rate limiter can write 300-500MB/s and cause short stalls.

You want an upstream that answers bugs. This repo is archived with 237 open issues and PRs, so you depend on Percona Server or MariaDB builds and their tuning expertise. Tuning also takes expertise: the wiki calls the defaults (4MB SST files, 4KB blocks) too small, and Percona's benchmark used settings supplied by Meta's MyRocks team.

integration.form: module — a MySQL storage-engine plugin compiled into Meta's MySQL server fork (a static, mandatory rocksdb_se plugin by default; ROCKSDB_DYNAMIC_PLUGIN builds a loadable module). You deploy the whole server, or use the MyRocks packaged in Percona Server / MariaDB.
integration.dependencies: RocksDB (git submodule), Boost (submodule) and zlib. Optional: LZ4, ZSTD, Snappy, BZip2, jemalloc, liburing, TBB, folly/glog, and Faiss (submodule, only with WITH_FB_VECTORDB). Plus the usual MySQL build dependencies (OpenSSL, bison, ncurses, libaio).
integration.min_toolchain: fb-mysql-8.0.32: GCC 7.1+ or Clang 5+ (enforced in cmake/os/Linux.cmake), CMake 3.5.1+ (higher minimums on some platforms). The 5.6-era wiki lists gcc 4.9/5.4/6.1 and Clang 3.9 as internally verified.
integration.platforms: POSIX only (the CMake hard-codes ROCKSDB_PLATFORM_POSIX; no Windows). Linux x86-64 is the tested target: the wiki officially supports CentOS 6.8/7.2 and Ubuntu 14.04-16.04 on a best-effort basis. Darwin build paths exist, and big-endian test failures are an open issue (#600).
integration.thread_safety: Handled by the server. Concurrent sessions go through RocksDB's TransactionDB with pessimistic row locks (per-session rocksdb_lock_wait_timeout, WRITE_COMMITTED write policy by default). Jan 2025 commits made parts of Rdb_transaction safe to access from other threads. There is no library-level API.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same SQL, protocol and replication, and you switch per table with ENGINE=RocksDB or ALTER TABLE. But foreign keys, fulltext/spatial indexes, savepoints and gap locks are missing, REPEATABLE-READ means snapshot isolation, row-based binlog is required, and the wiki calls mixing InnoDB and MyRocks in one instance 'not really transactional' and not for production.

gotchas: REPEATABLE-READ is PostgreSQL-style snapshot isolation, not InnoDB's gap-lock RR. Locking reads do not block phantoms, and statement-based binlog on a source can diverge replicas. Percona Server 5.7 rejected SELECT ... FOR UPDATE under RR, which is why the benchmark ran READ-COMMITTED (the tuning wiki recommends RC anyway).

rocksdb_bulk_load disables unique checks and enables commit-in-the-middle, so a bulk load is neither atomic nor duplicate-checked, and ingested key ranges must not overlap existing data. Open issue #1249 reports ALTER TABLE ... ENGINE=RocksDB from MyISAM finishing 'successfully' with an empty table when the merge buffer was too small (Percona 5.7). The fix was raising rocksdb_merge_buf_size.
Scan direction is fixed per column family when the table is created. Forward scans are fast and backward scans are slow, unless you put the index in a 'rev:' family, which reverses the trade-off.

Memory can exceed block cache plus memtables. Issue #1269 saw RSS grow from 95G to 120G after mass TTL compactions (resolved via TCMALLOC_RELEASE_RATE or by disabling TTL compaction). In issue #814 the server could not reopen RocksDB after an OOM kill. A maintainer blames a partially written WAL under rocksdb_wal_recovery_mode=1, and the tuning wiki sets it to 2.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick MyRocks when you need a MySQL-compatible transactional SQL engine with replication, not an embedded store: TerarkDB and TidesDB are RocksDB-class key-value libraries, and redb and libmdbx are embedded B-tree KV stores, so each would need its own SQL layer. The only sibling that is also a write-optimized MySQL engine is TokuDB/PerconaFT; MyRocks is the one proven at Meta's UDB scale, and Percona's current docs (9.7 branch) still cover it.
verified_claims_summary: Percona's Vadim Tkachenko ran sysbench-tpcc (100 warehouses x 10 tables, 56 threads, 1-hour runs averaged over the last 1600 s, READ-COMMITTED, no FKs, ROW binlog with sync_binlog=10000, direct I/O on both engines) on packaged Percona Server 5.7.21-20. The box had 2x Xeon E5-2683 v3 (28 cores), 256GB RAM and a Samsung SM863 SSD, and the cache was swept from 5GB to 100GB. MyRocks averaged 4206 tps vs InnoDB's 849 at 5GB (~5x), the gap closed to 1.16x at 50GB, and InnoDB led from 60GB (~1.30x at 80-100GB). No compiler or build flags were given, and the binary was not built from this repo.
status_note: The public repo is archived (last commit 2025-01-27 on fb-mysql-8.0.32, 237 open issues and PRs), though Meta presented new MyRocks features at FOSDEM 2025 (Faiss vectors, Thrift NoSQL access, user-defined timestamps). It is a GPLv2 MySQL server fork with Oracle's linking exception, so in practice you consume it through Percona Server or MariaDB rather than vendoring code.
